artifacts.summary: Verifies both entries against the live BimodalLogic tree: confirms Entry 1's f-now-exists / mid-vs-back-fwd split but recommends keeping it blocked since the mid clause's own discharge is scoped to an A1 instance no example occupies; finds Entry 2's dispatch-proposed replacement blocker (three tasks, all not-started) is itself stale -- one is abandoned, one is completed -- and identifies the correct current blocker as tasks 696 and a newly created task 703, per a same-day upstream survey that names this task by number; fully verifies the shape/reflexivity root-cause correction by declaration name.

next_steps: Run /plan 217 to create implementation plan for rewriting the two specs/state.json entries

memory_candidates.content: When a task dispatch's own description names specific upstream successor tasks as the corrected blocker, re-verify each named task's current status directly in the upstream repo's specs/state.json rather than trusting the dispatch text -- the dispatch can itself go stale between authoring and dispatch if the upstream repo is under concurrent active development (observed: two of three named tasks had already changed status -- one abandoned/folded, one completed -- before the dispatch even ran, and a fourth, newly-created task had already superseded the account).

When an upstream theorem's adequacy row states a discharge as holding 'at A1's restricted scope' (or similar scope qualifier), check whether the consuming repository's actual test/example inventory instantiates that scope before treating the discharge as actionable -- a magnitude-only half of a bound can be technically satisfiable while still resting on a theorem instance (e.g. empty-premise, single-conclusion) that zero real examples occupy, making the practical adequacy of using it currently unjustified.
